guide.title: A pattern and a place
guide.text: A constellation is a named area of sky. Its familiar connect-the-dots picture helps us find it, but the boundary defines which objects belong to that constellation. Different cultures draw different pictures among the stars.

guide.title: Stars can look close together
guide.text: The stars in a pattern can be very far apart in space. A constellation has no single distance from Earth. An asterism is a recognizable pattern, such as the Big Dipper within Ursa Major or the Summer Triangle across three constellations.

guide.title: A light-year measures distance
guide.text: One light-year is how far light travels in one year. Light from an object 100 light-years away takes about 100 years to reach us, so we see that object as it was in the past.

guide.title: Read the chart
guide.text: Bigger star dots mean brighter stars, not physically larger stars. The numbered scale is apparent magnitude: lower numbers mean brighter objects as seen from Earth. City lights can hide the fainter stars.

guide.title: Find your way around
guide.text: Right ascension (RA) runs around the sky in hours, from 0 to 24. Declination runs north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator in degrees. These coordinates are the sky’s version of longitude and latitude. J2000 tells you the reference frame used by these charts.

guide.title: Check the time and place
guide.text: A chart is a map, not a live view of tonight’s sky. What you can see changes with the date, time and your location. Start with a bright star or familiar pattern, then match nearby stars to the chart.

guide.title: Along the Sun’s path
guide.text: The ecliptic is the Sun’s apparent yearly path against the stars. It crosses 13 constellations, including Ophiuchus. The atlas’s Sun’s path filter uses these astronomical regions; they differ from the 12 equal signs used in astrology.

And.title: Another galaxy in view
And.text: This spiral galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away. Under a dark sky, you can see it without a telescope as a faint patch of light. It is a separate galaxy, far beyond the stars that draw Andromeda’s pattern.

Her.title: A crowded star cluster
Her.text: M13 is a globular cluster: a dense, roughly round gathering of stars. It lies about 25,000 light-years away and can be spotted with binoculars. A telescope reveals more of its crowded stars.

Lyr.title: A star’s glowing farewell
Lyr.text: The Ring Nebula is material shed by an aging Sun-like star, about 2,000 light-years away. Find its position between Sheliak and Sulafat on the chart. A telescope is needed to see its ring-like detail.

Ori.title: A place where stars are born
Ori.text: Look below Orion’s three-star belt for M42, a cloud of gas and dust where new stars form. From a dark site, it can be seen without a telescope. Binoculars or a telescope help reveal its hazy shape.

Sgr.title: A glowing stellar nursery
Sgr.text: The Lagoon Nebula is a star-forming cloud in Sagittarius. Hot young stars make its gas glow. Binoculars or a small telescope help you find it under dark skies; the colorful detail in space-telescope photos will look much subtler through an eyepiece.

Ser.title: Home of the Pillars of Creation
Ser.text: M16 includes a young star cluster and the Eagle Nebula in Serpens. The famous Pillars of Creation are part of this star-forming cloud. A small telescope can show the cluster; the pillars themselves are much harder to observe.

Tau.title: The remains of an exploded star
Tau.text: The Crab Nebula is the remnant of a supernova recorded in 1054. A rapidly spinning neutron star lies inside it. Despite its name, this object is in Taurus, not Cancer, the Crab. A telescope is needed to spot the nebula.

Cas.title: A bubble blown by a star
Cas.text: Cassiopeia’s familiar W-shaped pattern points you toward a region rich in stars. The Bubble Nebula is a cloud of gas and dust shaped by a massive star. This faint object is a telescope target, rather than something to expect with your eyes alone.

Aql.title: One corner of a larger pattern
Aql.text: Find Altair on Aquila’s chart. Together with Deneb in Cygnus and Vega in Lyra, it forms the Summer Triangle. The triangle is an asterism that spans three constellations.

Cyg.title: Follow the Summer Triangle
Cyg.text: Deneb in Cygnus forms one corner of the Summer Triangle. The other two corners are Vega in Lyra and Altair in Aquila. This large pattern can help you connect three separate constellations on the sky.

UMa.title: The Dipper is part of the Bear
UMa.text: The seven-star Big Dipper is a familiar pattern within Ursa Major. It is an asterism, while Ursa Major is the larger official constellation. Compare the Dipper’s outline with the constellation’s full boundary on the chart.
